name: Catalytic Chemistry
tagline: Accelerating reactions through homogeneous, heterogeneous, and biocatalysis.
seo_title: Catalytic Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Catalytic Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in homogeneous, heterogeneous, enzymatic, photo- and electrocatalysis.

definition.lead: Catalysis speeds up chemical reactions without the catalyst being used up, and it can steer them toward one product.
definition.body: Most industrial chemical processes rely on at least one catalyst, from fertilizer and fuels to plastics and medicines. Enzymes, metal complexes, solid surfaces and small organic molecules can all play the role.

facts.label: Fritz Haber demonstrates catalytic ammonia synthesis

branches.name: Homogeneous catalysis
branches.summary: Catalysts dissolved in the same phase as the reactants, often metal complexes.

branches.name: Heterogeneous catalysis
branches.summary: Solid catalysts working at their surface.
branches.example: The iron catalyst of the Haber–Bosch process.

branches.name: Biocatalysis
branches.summary: Enzymes as catalysts, natural or engineered.
branches.example: Enzymes in laundry detergents and drug manufacture.

branches.name: Organocatalysis
branches.summary: Small organic molecules as catalysts, without metals.

branches.name: Electrocatalysis
branches.summary: Catalysts that speed up electrode reactions.

branches.name: Asymmetric catalysis
branches.summary: Catalysts that make one mirror-image product.

branches.name: Industrial catalysis
branches.summary: Catalysts that run refineries and chemical plants.

timeline.title: Catalysis is named
timeline.text: Jöns Jacob Berzelius coins 'catalysis' for reactions sped up by substances that are not consumed.
timeline.why: Gave a name to a phenomenon seen in many labs.

timeline.title: Ammonia from air
timeline.text: Fritz Haber demonstrates catalytic ammonia synthesis; Carl Bosch scales it up.
timeline.why: Fertilizer that now helps feed much of humanity.

timeline.title: Hydrogenation
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Paul Sabatier for hydrogenation with finely divided metals, shared with Victor Grignard.
timeline.why: The basis of margarine and many industrial reductions.

timeline.title: Fischer–Tropsch
timeline.text: Franz Fischer and Hans Tropsch convert carbon monoxide and hydrogen into liquid hydrocarbons.
timeline.why: Synthetic fuels from coal, gas or biomass.

timeline.title: Ziegler catalysts
timeline.text: Karl Ziegler makes polyethylene at low pressure with metal catalysts; Giulio Natta extends it to polypropylene.
timeline.why: Shaped the modern plastics industry; Nobel Prize in 1963.

timeline.title: Catalytic converters
timeline.text: Cars in the United States begin to use catalytic converters.
timeline.why: Cut emissions of carbon monoxide and unburned fuel.

timeline.title: Asymmetric catalysis
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Knowles, Noyori and Sharpless.

timeline.title: Surfaces explained
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Gerhard Ertl for studies of chemical processes on solid surfaces.
timeline.why: Revealed step by step how the Haber–Bosch catalyst works.

timeline.title: Evolving enzymes
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Frances Arnold for the directed evolution of enzymes.
timeline.why: Enzymes tailored for green industrial chemistry.

timeline.title: Organocatalysis
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to Benjamin List and David MacMillan.
timeline.why: Cheap, metal-free catalysts for asymmetric synthesis.

options: Speeds up a reaction and is regenerated
quiz.explain: It offers a lower-energy path and comes back unchanged at the end of each cycle.

options: In a different phase from the reactants
In the same phase as the reactants
quiz.explain: Typically a solid with gases or liquids flowing over it.

quiz.q: The Haber–Bosch process uses a catalyst based on…
quiz.explain: Promoted iron catalysts make ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.

quiz.q: The turnover number of a catalyst is…
options: Moles of product made per mole of catalyst before it dies
The temperature at which the catalyst works best
The number of steps in the catalytic cycle
The mass of catalyst needed per litre of solvent
quiz.explain: A high turnover number means a little catalyst goes a long way.

quiz.q: Which metals do car catalytic converters use?
quiz.explain: They oxidize CO and hydrocarbons and reduce nitrogen oxides.

options: A substance binds strongly to the active sites and blocks them
The catalyst gets too hot and melts
The catalyst dissolves into the product
The catalyst turns into an enzyme over time
quiz.explain: Leaded petrol, for example, poisons catalytic converters.
A few catalysts in cells, called ribozymes, are made of RNA.

quiz.q: Organocatalysis, recognized with the 2021 Nobel Prize, uses…
options: Visible light with no catalyst at all
quiz.explain: Molecules like the amino acid proline can catalyse asymmetric reactions.

quiz.q: Ziegler–Natta catalysts are used to make…
quiz.explain: They grow polymer chains at metal centres.

quiz.q: Frances Arnold's 2018 Nobel Prize was for…
quiz.explain: She used cycles of mutation and selection to create better enzymes.

quiz.q: Why are converter catalysts spread on a honeycomb structure?
options: To maximize the surface area in contact with the gas
Only to reduce the weight of the car
To make the converter look more modern
To cool the exhaust gas before it leaves
quiz.explain: Heterogeneous catalysis happens only at the surface.
Berzelius also introduced modern chemical symbols.
